questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Setting AI tolerances
questions.question: A legal aid charity's board states a low appetite for its eligibility-screening model wrongly rejecting people who qualify for help. Which tolerance would the IS auditor consider BEST for senior management to set within it?

options.A: At least 95% overall accuracy on the screening model's held-out test data
options.B: A screening-results report to the board at the end of each quarter
options.C: No more than 1 in 100 qualifying applicants screened out each month
options.D: A pledge that every applicant is treated fairly and with respect

questions.key_concept: A tolerance turns appetite into a measurable limit on the harm itself; overall accuracy can stay high while that harm grows.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option could actually tell management when the board's appetite is being breached.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance sets a measurable limit, within appetite, on the harm the board named: people who qualify being wrongly rejected. A monthly cap on such rejections can be monitored and escalated. Overall accuracy, option A, is the runner-up: it is measurable, but it blends all errors, so it can stay at 95% while far more qualifying applicants are screened out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is precise and measurable. But overall accuracy mixes all errors, so it can hold steady while qualifying applicants are wrongly rejected.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the board needs visibility. But a report is a way to monitor a limit, not the limit itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fairness matters here. But a pledge restates the appetite in softer words; a tolerance must be a limit someone can measure.

tips: Eliminate: D restates intent without a measure, and B is a reporting step, which monitors a limit rather than setting one.
Final two: C beats A because a tolerance limits the named harm directly; overall accuracy can stay high while wrongful rejections rise.
Exam cue: a good AI tolerance measures the harm in the appetite statement, not a general model metric like accuracy.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Multi-model decisions
questions.question: An immigration service runs visa applications through three models; a flag from any one sends a case toward refusal, and each meets its own wrongful-flag tolerance. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Applicants may not know which of the three models flagged them
options.B: Wrongful flags across all three models together may exceed appetite
options.C: The three models may be retrained on different schedules
options.D: Each model may run on a different hosting platform

questions.key_concept: When several models feed one decision, their errors combine; tolerances must also cover the end-to-end outcome for the people affected.
questions.pre_read: Follow one applicant through every model, and ask how the chances of a wrong flag add up along the way.
questions.correct_explanation: Because a flag from any one model pushes a case toward refusal, an applicant faces three chances of a wrongful flag. Each model can meet its own tolerance while the combined rate is much higher, and per-model limits would never show it. Unclear sources of flags, option A, is the runner-up: it weakens appeals, but it does not show whether combined harm stays within appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because applicants need to know what to appeal. But transparency helps challenge one case; it does not show whether combined wrongful flags stay within appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retraining is a change to control. But differing schedules are a change-management detail; they do not reveal the combined error rate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because platforms affect resilience. But where each model runs says nothing about how many applicants are wrongly pushed toward refusal.

tips: Eliminate: C is a change-management detail, and D is a hosting question; neither shows how many applicants are wrongly pushed toward refusal.
Final two: B beats A because separate tolerances can each be met while combined wrongful flags exceed appetite; transparency helps appeals, not measurement.
Exam cue: when models are chained into one decision, check that someone measures the end-to-end error for the people affected, not just each model.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Vendor exit and continuity
questions.question: A veterinary diagnostics lab licenses a vendor's AI model that reads blood smears; the continuity clause escrows the model's source code if the vendor fails. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the penalty the vendor pays if the service fails
options.B: Require the vendor's annual controls report covering its data centers
options.C: Test the escrow release process with the agent every year
options.D: Extend escrow to the trained model files and their configuration

questions.key_concept: Source code alone cannot rebuild a trained model; AI continuity needs the trained model files, configuration and, where possible, data.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the lab would actually need to keep reading smears if the vendor disappeared tomorrow.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's behavior lives in its trained parameters, not only in its code; rebuilding it from code would need the original training data, compute and expertise, and would still give a different model. Escrow must cover the trained model files and configuration. Testing the release process, option C, is the runner-up: it proves the agent can release what is held, but what is held cannot run the lab's tests.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because penalties motivate vendors. But money after a failure does not keep the lab's blood tests running.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because controls reports are standard vendor assurance. But data center controls say nothing about whether the lab could run the model if the vendor failed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because untested escrow often fails. But a smooth release of source code alone still leaves the lab without a working trained model.

tips: Eliminate: B covers the vendor's data centers rather than continuity of the model, and A pays compensation after failure without keeping the tests running.
Final two: D beats C because testing release of source code proves nothing if code cannot rebuild the trained model the lab depends on.
Exam cue: for AI continuity, the asset to protect is the trained model and its configuration, not just the code that built it.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Vendors using other AI providers
questions.question: A wealth manager's reporting vendor discloses that it now sends client portfolio data to another firm's language model to draft commentary. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important to confirm?

options.A: Whether the model provider may keep or train on client data
options.B: Whether the vendor's controls report now covers the model provider
options.C: Whether the vendor encrypts data it sends to the model provider
options.D: Whether the vendor accepts liability for the commentary's content

questions.key_concept: When a vendor passes data to another AI provider, first confirm whether that provider may retain or train on it; accountability stays with the buyer.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the client data goes next, and ask what the new party is allowed to do with it.
questions.correct_explanation: Client data now reaches a fourth party outside the original due diligence. Many model providers' terms allow them to keep inputs or use them to improve their models, which could expose confidential portfolios far beyond the original purpose. Controls-report coverage, option B, is the runner-up: it matters for assurance, but such reports cover the provider's environment, not whether its terms permit training on client data.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because controls reports are standard vendor assurance. But they cover operations and security, not whether the provider's terms let it keep or train on client data.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption protects data in transit. But it secures delivery; it does not limit what the provider may do with data once received.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because commentary errors could mislead clients. But accountability for client communications stays with the wealth manager; a liability clause cannot transfer it.

tips: Eliminate: D seeks to transfer accountability, which stays with the wealth manager, and C protects data in transit without limiting what the provider may do with it.
Final two: A beats B because the first question is what the provider may do with client data; controls reports cover its environment, not its terms of use.
Exam cue: when AI adds a party to the data flow, ask first whether that party may keep or train on the data, then how it is protected.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Data quality for training
questions.question: A bus operator will redesign routes with a demand model trained on trips logged in its smartphone app, data its owner has checked as complete and accurate. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The app's trip records may not be encrypted while stored
options.B: Riders' habits may shift once the redesigned routes begin
options.C: Riders who never use the app are absent from the training data
options.D: The quality checks were run by the owner rather than independently

questions.key_concept: Data can be complete and accurate yet unrepresentative; quality rules for training data must ask who is missing from it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who uses the bus but would never appear in the data the model learned from.
questions.correct_explanation: Records can be complete and accurate for app users while leaving out every rider who pays cash or has no smartphone, often older or lower-income people. Routes planned from that data may serve them worse. Quality rules must cover representativeness. Independent checks, option D, are the runner-up: independence strengthens evidence, but checking completeness and accuracy again would not reveal who is missing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because trip data needs protection. But encryption is a security control; it does not change who the training data leaves out.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because habits change with new routes. But that is a later monitoring question; the data is skewed before any route changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners checking their own data is weaker evidence. But an independent check of completeness and accuracy would still miss riders the app never records.

tips: Eliminate: A is a security control that leaves the data's coverage unchanged, and B is a later monitoring question, while the skew exists now.
Final two: C beats D because rechecking completeness and accuracy, however independently, cannot show riders the app never captured; representativeness is a separate test.
Exam cue: complete and accurate is not the same as representative; ask who never appears in the data the model learned from.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Reusing operational data
questions.question: A toll-road operator's data scientists have copied plate-camera records, collected to bill drivers, into a training set for a model predicting commuters' daily routes. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the team pseudonymize plate numbers before training continues
options.B: Have the data owner decide whether billing data may serve this purpose
options.C: Have the team record the copy's lineage in the data catalog
options.D: Have IT restrict the training set to the data science team

questions.key_concept: Data collected for one purpose cannot be reused to train a model until its owner approves the new purpose under the collection terms.
questions.pre_read: Compare why the data was collected with what it is now being used for, and ask who can approve the difference.
questions.correct_explanation: The records were collected to bill drivers; predicting commuters' routes is a new purpose that may not fit the collection terms and can reveal where people live and work. The data owner must decide, with privacy advice, whether the purpose is permitted before training goes on. Recording lineage, option C, is the runner-up: it documents where the copy came from, but a record does not make the use permitted.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it lowers identification risk. But daily routes can still point to individuals, and protecting data does not make a new use permitted.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because lineage is core data governance. But recording where the copy came from does not decide whether training on it is allowed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because limiting access reduces exposure. But it secures the copy without deciding whether the data may be used to train this model.

tips: Eliminate: D secures the copy without settling whether it may be used, and A pseudonymizes plates, though routes still identify drivers and protection never permits a use.
Final two: B beats C because lineage records the copy but cannot approve it; the data owner must first decide whether billing data may train this model.
Exam cue: data held for one purpose is not free to train any model; expect the data owner to approve the new purpose first.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Assistants that search internal files
questions.question: A seafood exporter's internal AI assistant answers any employee's questions from an index of the whole shared drive, including HR disciplinary files only HR may open. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT encrypt the assistant's document index at rest
options.B: Have IT add an output filter that masks employee names in answers
options.C: Have HR remind staff not to ask the assistant about colleagues
options.D: Have the owner limit answers to files each user may access

questions.key_concept: Retrieval-based AI must enforce each user's existing access rights, or it can reveal personal data that users could never open directly.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the assistant applies the same access rules as the shared drive when it answers a question.
questions.correct_explanation: The index lets the assistant draw on HR disciplinary files when anyone asks, so staff can learn about colleagues' cases they could never open directly. Answers must respect each user's existing permissions. A name-masking filter, option B, is the runner-up: it reduces exposure, but details of a case can still identify the person, and the assistant still reads files the user may not see.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects stored data. But the assistant decrypts the index to answer, so encryption does nothing about who receives the answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because output filters are a common AI safeguard. But case details can identify people without names, and the assistant still draws on files the user may not see.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because guidance shapes behavior. But a reminder relies on every user's restraint, and curious or careless questions would still return HR details.

tips: Eliminate: A encrypts an index the assistant must decrypt to answer, and C relies on users' restraint rather than a control on what the assistant returns.
Final two: D beats B because enforcing existing permissions stops the exposure at its source; masking names still leaves identifying case details in answers.
Exam cue: for AI that answers from internal documents, check that retrieval enforces each user's existing access before adding filters or reminders.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Assessing a chatbot's privacy
questions.question: A wildlife charity's privacy impact assessment for its donor chatbot was completed by the security team and covers only encryption and access to stored records. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the privacy officer extend it to prompts, outputs and logs
options.B: Have the vendor certify that the chatbot complies with privacy laws
options.C: Have the security team add penetration tests of the chatbot
options.D: Have the security team encrypt chat logs as well as stored records

questions.key_concept: A privacy impact assessment for AI covers personal data in prompts, outputs and logs, and is owned by privacy roles, not only security.
questions.pre_read: List every place donors' personal data can enter or leave the chatbot, then compare that list with what the assessment covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Donors may type personal details into the chatbot, its answers can reveal them, and chat logs keep them. A privacy impact assessment must cover purpose, consent, retention and those flows, and privacy roles own it. Encrypting chat logs too, option D, is the runner-up: it notices the logs, but it treats privacy as security and still skips purpose, retention and outputs.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certification sounds conclusive. But a vendor's claim is an input, and it cannot assess how this charity uses donors' data.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because testing finds weaknesses. But penetration tests are a security control; they do not assess how donors' personal data is used.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it extends protection to chat logs. But encryption guards against outsiders; it does not assess purpose, retention or what the chatbot reveals.

tips: Eliminate: C adds security testing to a privacy gap, and B relies on a vendor's claim, which cannot assess the charity's own use of donor data.
Final two: A beats D because privacy needs purpose, retention and output checks owned by privacy roles; encrypting logs is still a security answer.
Exam cue: when a privacy assessment of AI covers only security controls, expect privacy owners to extend it to prompts, outputs and logs.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Testing for memorized data
questions.question: A hearing-aid clinic chain fine-tuned a generative model on patients' past emails to draft replies. Before release, which evidence would BEST show the IS auditor that the model will not reveal patients' personal details?

options.A: The vendor's statement that its base model protects personal details
options.B: The output filter's settings for blocking phone numbers and addresses
options.C: Results of extraction tests probing for memorized patient details
options.D: Confirmation that the patient emails were deleted after fine-tuning

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuned models can memorize training text; tests that try to extract it show whether personal data could leak in outputs.
questions.pre_read: Ask where patients' details could still exist after training, and which evidence actually probes that place.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning on a small, distinctive set such as patient emails raises the chance the model memorizes and repeats details. Extraction tests that prompt the model to reproduce training text show directly whether it leaks. The output filter's settings, option B, are the runner-up: a filter helps, but settings show intent, not behavior, and pattern blocking misses names and hearing conditions.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor built the base model. But its statement covers the base model, not memorization from the clinic's own fine-tuning data.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because filters are a common output control. But settings show what was configured, not what leaks; names and hearing conditions match no phone-number pattern.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because deleting source data seems final. But a model keeps what it memorized during fine-tuning, so deletion says nothing about its outputs.

tips: Eliminate: D deletes the source but not what the model memorized, and A covers the vendor's base model, not the clinic's fine-tuning on patient emails.
Final two: C beats B because extraction tests show what the model actually reveals; filter settings show intent and miss details that fit no pattern.
Exam cue: to show a generative model will not leak training data, prefer tests that try to extract it over settings, deletions or vendor claims.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Erasure decisions for models
questions.question: A podcast app's data team decided alone that erased users' reviews, a tiny share of its generative model's training data, need no model action. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data team retrain the model after every erasure request
options.B: Have the model owner decide, with the privacy officer confirming
options.C: Have IT confirm the users' reviews were deleted from every system
options.D: Have the data team record its reasoning in the erasure log

questions.key_concept: Whether erasure requires model action is the model owner's decision, confirmed by privacy; a small share of data does not rule out memorization.
questions.pre_read: Ask who should own a decision about a legal duty, and whether the reason given actually holds for generative models.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative models can memorize even data that appears in few training examples, so a tiny share is no proof the reviews are gone. Whether to retrain, filter outputs or record low risk is the model owner's decision, with the privacy officer confirming it meets the legal duty. Recording the reasoning, option D, is the runner-up: it creates a trail, but the flawed decision stays with the builders.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining removes the data. But retraining after every request is costly and not always required; the owner weighs retraining, filtering or recorded low risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because complete deletion seems to answer the request. But deleting source reviews does not remove what the trained model may have memorized.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because documented decisions can be reviewed. But recording a flawed share-based argument leaves the builders deciding a legal duty without the owner or privacy.

tips: Eliminate: A mandates retraining for every request, which the owner should weigh case by case, and C deletes source reviews, which does not touch what the model memorized.
Final two: B beats D because memorization can occur even for rare examples, so the decision needs the accountable owner and privacy sign-off, not a recorded builders' guess.
Exam cue: after an erasure request, the model owner decides what happens to trained models, with privacy confirming; data share alone proves nothing.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Replacing a scoring method
questions.question: A development agency replaced its points-based grant scoring with a model 6% more accurate at predicting business survival; rejected applicants are entitled to reasons. Which question should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Whether the model can still give rejected applicants meaningful reasons
options.B: Whether the agency's systems can score applicants as fast as before
options.C: Whether the 6% gain held on data kept back from the builders
options.D: Whether the old points rules were archived for future audits

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy-AI characteristics trade off; a gain in accuracy cannot override an explainability requirement owed to the people affected.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the agency owes each rejected applicant, and whether the new model can still provide it.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST notes that accuracy and interpretability can trade off. Here the agency owes every rejected applicant reasons, so a more accurate model that cannot produce meaningful ones fails a requirement, whatever its gain. Confirming the 6% on unseen data, option C, is the runner-up: it tests whether the gain is real, but a real gain still would not meet the duty to explain.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complex models need capacity. But speed is an operational question; it does not affect what the agency owes rejected applicants.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because claimed gains need independent proof. But even a confirmed 6% gain would not let the agency give rejected applicants the reasons they are owed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because records support later review. But archiving old rules concerns past decisions; it does not show the new model can explain new ones.

tips: Eliminate: B is an operational speed question, and D preserves old rules for past decisions; neither shows the new model can explain its rejections.
Final two: A beats C because a confirmed accuracy gain still cannot meet the duty to give reasons; explainability here is a requirement, not a preference.
Exam cue: when a more accurate model replaces an explainable one, check first whether the people affected can still get the explanations they are owed.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Criteria for AI principles
questions.question: A ferry operator's AI principles say its booking chatbot must be transparent. Which owner-set criterion would BEST let the IS auditor test that principle?

options.A: The vendor publishes an annual transparency report on its model
options.B: Passenger satisfaction with the chatbot stays above 85 percent
options.C: The chatbot is designed to be open and honest with passengers
options.D: Every chat starts by telling passengers they are talking to AI

questions.key_concept: A principle becomes auditable when owners state it as a specific, observable criterion for the use, such as disclosure in every chat.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask whether a tester could check it in this chatbot and record a clear pass or fail.
questions.correct_explanation: Transparency in the NIST framework concerns what information about an AI system is available to the people interacting with it. A rule that every chat opens by saying the passenger is talking to AI is specific to this use and can be checked chat by chat. The vendor's report, option A, is the runner-up: it informs about the model generally, but says nothing testable about this chatbot.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is published and independent of the operator. But it describes the vendor's model in general, not what passengers are told in this chatbot.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is measurable. But satisfaction measures how passengers feel, not whether they know they are dealing with AI.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sounds like the principle. But a design aim restates the principle; it gives a tester nothing measurable to check.

tips: Eliminate: C restates the principle without anything to measure, and B measures satisfaction, which says nothing about whether passengers know they face AI.
Final two: D beats A because a criterion must be testable in this use; a vendor's general report cannot be checked against this chatbot.
Exam cue: a good AI criterion is specific to the use and observable, so a tester can record pass or fail for each case.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Uses outside a law's scope
questions.question: Counsel confirms a supermarket chain's pricing model is outside a new AI law, so the AI committee proposes dropping planned checks for unfair prices in low-income areas. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Ask the regulator to confirm the model is out of scope
options.B: Drop the checks, since the law sets the required standard
options.C: Keep the checks as part of managing the model's risk to shoppers
options.D: Have counsel recheck the law's scope at each annual compliance review

questions.key_concept: Legal compliance is a floor: an AI use outside one law still answers to other laws, the organization's principles and its risk appetite.
questions.pre_read: Ask what besides this one law should govern how the model treats shoppers.
questions.correct_explanation: Being outside one AI law removes that law's duties, not the risk that the model charges low-income neighborhoods more, which other laws and the chain's own risk management may still need to address. Rechecking the law each year, option D, is the runner-up: monitoring scope is sensible, but it still treats one law as the only reason to check for unfair prices.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a regulator's view is authoritative. But confirming the model is out of scope again leaves the harm to low-income shoppers unchecked.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because counsel has confirmed scope. But one law is a floor; other laws and the chain's own risk limits still apply to unfair pricing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because laws change and scope can shift. But rechecking scope still treats one law as the only reason to test for unfair prices.

tips: Eliminate: B treats one law as the whole standard, though it is only a floor, and A seeks more certainty about scope while the pricing harm goes unchecked.
Final two: C beats D because the checks address a harm to shoppers that exists whatever the law's scope; rechecking scope only tracks legal duty.
Exam cue: being outside one AI law does not end the duty to manage harm; expect checks to follow risk to people, not just legal scope.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Deciding which laws apply
questions.question: A cosmetics retailer's app uses a vendor's skin-analysis model, and the vendor says a new AI law's high-risk rules do not apply. Who should the IS auditor expect to hold PRIMARY responsibility for that judgment?

options.A: The AI governance committee, voting on the vendor's assessment
options.B: The retailer's legal counsel, advised by the model owner
options.C: The IS auditor, after testing the model's controls in the app
options.D: The vendor, which built the model and knows its design best

questions.key_concept: Whether an AI law applies depends on the organization's own use and market; that is a legal judgment for its counsel, not the vendor.
questions.pre_read: Separate who built the model from who uses it, and ask whose use the law's duties attach to.
questions.correct_explanation: Applicability turns on how, where and for whom the retailer uses the model, which the retailer knows best, so it is a legal judgment for the retailer's counsel, informed by the model owner's description of the use. The AI governance committee, option A, is the runner-up: it approves high-impact uses and acts on the answer, but a vote cannot replace a legal judgment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the committee governs AI uses. But applicability is a legal judgment; the committee acts on counsel's answer rather than voting on a vendor's view.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors assess compliance. But applicability is a legal judgment for counsel; the auditor later tests the mapping and evidence rather than making the call.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor knows the model's design. But duties attach to how the retailer uses it, and a vendor's view is an input, not a judgment.

tips: Eliminate: D leaves applicability to the vendor, whose view is only an input, and C has the auditor making a call it must later assess.
Final two: B beats A because applicability is a legal judgment about the retailer's own use; the committee acts on that answer rather than replacing it.
Exam cue: who decides whether an AI law applies? Legal counsel, using the owner's account of the use; vendors advise and auditors test.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Certificates offered by vendors
questions.question: A contract-cleaning company's vendor offers its certified AI management system as evidence that its shift-matching model treats cleaners fairly. What is the IS auditor's MOST appropriate conclusion?

options.A: The certificate shows the model's fairness was independently audited
options.B: The certificate is sufficient if the certifying body is accredited
options.C: The model's source code must be reviewed to judge its fairness
options.D: The certificate covers the vendor's processes, not this model's fairness

questions.key_concept: A management-system certificate covers how an organization runs AI governance within its scope, not whether a specific model is fair.
questions.pre_read: Ask what exactly the certificate's auditors examined, and whether that included this model's outcomes for cleaners.
questions.correct_explanation: Management-system certification shows the vendor runs an AI governance process that meets a standard within its scope; it does not test whether a given model's matches are fair. The company still needs model-level fairness results on data for its own cleaners. An accredited certifier, option B, is the runner-up: accreditation makes the certificate credible, but a credible certificate still covers process, not this model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because certification involves independent auditors. But they assess the management system within scope, not the fairness of each model's decisions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accreditation is a real quality check on certificates. But even a credible certificate covers the management process, not this model's outcomes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because code seems to reveal logic. But a learned model's behavior comes from training data and parameters; fairness is shown by testing outcomes.

tips: Eliminate: A reads a process certificate as a model audit, and C looks to source code, though a learned model's fairness shows in tested outcomes.
Final two: D beats B because accreditation makes a certificate credible but does not widen its scope; it still covers process, not this model.
Exam cue: a certified AI management system shows the process; model fairness needs model-level testing against defined criteria.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Applying the NIST AI RMF
questions.question: A ship classification society using the NIST AI RMF has tested its inspection-scheduling model for bias and robustness, but never documented its intended use, affected parties or tolerances. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner define the model's context of use before more testing
options.B: Have the team choose risk responses for the issues tests found
options.C: Have the society seek external certification of its AI management system
options.D: Have the team extend robustness testing to more attack types

questions.key_concept: In the NIST AI RMF, Map outcomes such as intended use, affected parties and tolerances are the basis for judging Measure results and Manage responses.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a tester needs to know before deciding whether a bias or robustness result is good enough.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST describes Map outcomes as the basis for Measure and Manage: without a documented intended use, affected parties and tolerances, nobody can say which test results matter or what level is acceptable. The owner should set that context first. Choosing risk responses, option B, is the runner-up: acting on findings seems decisive, but responses chosen without tolerances have nothing to aim at.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because findings call for action. But without tolerances and intended use, there is no basis for deciding which findings need a response or how much.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because certification sounds like assurance. But a management-system certificate covers process scope; it does not supply this model's missing context.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because broader testing finds more issues. But more tests without context produce more results nobody can judge against a purpose or tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: D adds tests that still lack a basis for judgment, and C seeks a process certificate, which cannot supply the model's missing context.
Final two: A beats B because responses need tolerances to aim at; Map outcomes are the basis for both Measure and Manage.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, expect context (intended use, affected people, tolerances) to be set before test results or responses are judged.
